note: Closes act 2 and the examinable scope. Table 8.4's four scheduling types and the paging/segmentation contrast (invisible versus visible to the programmer) are used as the book states them.

items.stem: In a batch system, what happens to a newly submitted job before it becomes a process?
items.correct: It is routed to disk and held in a batch queue until the long-term scheduler creates a process from it
distractors: It is loaded straight into main memory and given a time slice
It is executed immediately at the lowest available priority
It is held in main memory until an existing process terminates
items.rationale: The job waits on DISK, not in memory — that is what makes the long-term scheduler a control on the degree of multiprogramming. It makes two decisions: whether the system can take another process at all, and which job to admit.

items.stem: How does admission differ for interactive users in a time-sharing system compared with batch jobs?
items.correct: All authorised users are accepted until the system reaches a saturation measure, after which a request is refused with a message to try later
distractors: Interactive users are queued in the same way, but with higher priority
Interactive users are always admitted, and the system degrades gracefully
Interactive users bypass the long-term scheduler entirely
items.rationale: Time-sharing users are not simply queued and kept waiting — a person staring at a blank terminal is a worse outcome than an honest refusal. The saturation threshold is what turns an unbounded queue into a bounded one.
items.source: ch-08.md §8.2 — 'the OS will accept all authorized comers until the system is saturated'

items.stem: What problem does multiprogramming solve that a simple batch system leaves unsolved?
items.correct: A single process blocked on I/O leaves the processor idle; holding several processes in memory lets another run in the gap
distractors: It reduces the memory each individual process needs
It removes the need for the processor to handle interrupts
It guarantees each process a fixed share of processor time
items.rationale: This is the same efficiency argument as interrupts in chapter 3, one level up: the processor should not wait when there is other work available. Fixed shares are a scheduling POLICY, not the reason multiprogramming exists.
items.source: ch-08.md §8.1 — the evolution toward multiprogrammed batch systems

items.stem: According to Table 8.4, what decision does SHORT-TERM scheduling make?
items.correct: Which available process will be executed by the processor
distractors: Which jobs to add to the pool of processes to be executed
How many processes should be partially or fully in main memory
Which process's pending I/O request an available device should handle
items.rationale: The three distractors are the other three rows of the same table: long-term, medium-term and I/O scheduling. They are distinguished by WHAT is being decided, and the short-term scheduler is the one that runs most often.

items.stem: The long-term scheduler controls the degree of multiprogramming. What does that phrase mean?
items.correct: The number of processes in memory, which it sets by deciding how many jobs to admit
distractors: The number of processors available to run processes
The number of time slices each process receives per second
The proportion of memory allocated to the operating system
items.rationale: Admitting more jobs raises the degree of multiprogramming and with it the chance the processor always has work; admitting too many exhausts memory and drives swapping. The long-term scheduler is where that balance is struck.
items.source: ch-08.md §8.2 — 'it controls the degree of multiprogramming'

items.stem: Put the three process schedulers in order, from the one that runs least often to the one that runs most often.
items.rationale: The long-term scheduler acts when a job is admitted, controlling the degree of multiprogramming. The medium-term scheduler is part of the swapping function, deciding how many processes are in main memory. The short-term scheduler chooses which ready process runs next and acts most frequently of the three. The three operate on three different timescales, which is what separates them.

items.stem: Why is main memory partitioned at all in a multiprogramming system?
items.correct: Several processes must be resident at once, and each needs a region of memory that is its own
distractors: The processor can only address a limited amount of memory at a time
Partitioning is required for the cache to map addresses correctly
Each partition is served by a different memory bus
items.rationale: Multiprogramming requires several processes in memory simultaneously, and partitioning is how that space is divided and protected. Cache mapping and bus structure are organizational matters below this level and do not depend on partitioning.

items.stem: A fixed-partition scheme uses equal-size partitions. What waste does that guarantee?
items.correct: Any process smaller than its partition leaves the remainder unusable by anyone else
distractors: Gaps between partitions accumulate as processes come and go
Partitions must be recompacted periodically to remain contiguous
The partition table grows without bound as processes are created
items.rationale: Internal waste is inherent to fixed partitions: the unused tail of an occupied partition cannot be reallocated. The first two distractors describe what happens with VARIABLE partitions instead, where the gaps fall between allocations rather than inside them.
items.source: ch-08.md §8.3 — Partitioning, and Problem 8.4's fixed-partition scheme

items.stem: How does paging differ from segmentation in the programmer's view?
items.correct: Paging is invisible to the programmer; segmentation is usually visible and is provided as a convenience for organising programs and data
distractors: Both are invisible; the difference is only in how the hardware translates addresses
Paging is visible and segmentation invisible, which is why segments have no names
Both are visible, but only segmentation requires the programmer to manage it
items.rationale: This is the load-bearing distinction. Paging exists to give the programmer a LARGER address space without their involvement. Segmentation exists to let them organise that space and attach privilege and protection attributes to the parts.
items.source: ch-08.md §8.3 — 'paging is invisible to the programmer ... segmentation is usually visible'

items.stem: What form does a memory reference take under segmentation, and why?
items.correct: A (segment number, offset) pair, because segments are of variable and even dynamic size
distractors: A single linear address, because segments are contiguous in physical memory
A (page number, offset) pair, identical to paging
A (segment number, page number, offset) triple in every implementation
items.rationale: Segments vary in size, so the offset cannot be a fixed-width field carved from a linear address the way a page offset is — the two parts must be given explicitly. That variability is also why segmentation suffers external fragmentation where paging does not.
items.source: ch-08.md §8.3 — Segmentation, '(segment number, offset) form of address'

items.stem: Segmentation associates privilege and protection attributes with instructions and data. Why does segmentation support this more naturally than paging?
items.correct: A segment corresponds to a meaningful unit such as a procedure or a data structure, so a single access right describes something coherent
distractors: Pages cannot carry protection bits in hardware
Segments are always smaller than pages, so protection is finer grained
Paging places all of a process's data in one page by design
items.rationale: Protection is most useful when its unit matches a logical unit of the program. A page is an arbitrary fixed-size slice that may straddle two unrelated structures. Pages CAN carry protection bits — they just protect a region with no inherent meaning.
items.source: ch-08.md §8.3 — Segmentation, privilege and protection attributes

items.correct: A scheme in which a process's address space may exceed physical memory, with parts held on disk and brought in as referenced
distractors: A region of disk reserved as a permanent extension of main memory for all processes
A cache of recently used page table entries kept inside the processor
Memory shared between processes so they can communicate without copying
items.rationale: Virtual memory decouples the address space a program sees from the physical memory installed. The second distractor is the translation lookaside buffer, which SUPPORTS virtual memory — a component, not a definition.
